extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in the Charlie Hebdo attacks, satire, media and free-speech issues
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted evaluative principles and norms about producing and responding to satirical cartoons and humour — especially around depictions of religion, editorial choices, and the limits of free expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to parody / defence of satire
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle that satirists are 'beholden to the principle that every human being has the right to be parodied.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted in the article as a defence of satire (editor of Titanic): this frames parody as a legitimate practice that should not be halted even in the face of violent intimidation. Example/appeal: many cartoonists worldwide responded in solidarity; editorial positions defended publishing as an expression of free speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid gratuitous offensiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: ''Defending freedom of expression in the face of oppression is one thing; insisting on the right to be obnoxious and offensive just because you can is infantile.''
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attributed to Al Jazeera English editor Salah-Aldeen Khadr — used as a caution that exercising the right to offend should be weighed against purpose and value. Anti-pattern: producing intentionally shocking content with no critical or satirical aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use humour to address awkward subjects and perform social critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Cartoonists, writers and artists 'used their pens with a lot of humour to address sometimes awkward subjects and as such performed an essential function.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seen as a positive justification for satire: humour can tackle difficult/taboo issues and serve an essential democratic function (social critique, accountability). Example: defenders framed Charlie Hebdo's work as fulfilling this role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer targeting power/own politicians over venerated figures of other cultures
rubrics_metrics.description: ''I think it's a mistake to caricaturise the figures venerated by another culture. You shouldn't do it. Instead of doing something like that, you should first make caricatures of your own country's politicians.''
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hayao Miyazaki's comment used as prescriptive guidance for satirists: focus satire on domestic political figures or those in positions of power rather than religious figures deeply venerated by other communities. Anti-pattern: deliberately provoking other cultures by attacking their sacred figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid satire that degrades or functions like hate propaganda
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique that equates some of Charlie Hebdo's work with 'political pornography' that 'degrade[s], demean[s], humiliate[s] and insult[s] the people.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Norman Finkelstein's comparison to Der Stürmer is used to warn that satire can cross into dehumanising, hateful messaging. Evaluation criterion: does the humour attack power/ideas or does it stigmatise and dehumanise a group?

rubrics_metrics.name: Make satire meaningful rather than merely provocative or vapid
rubrics_metrics.description: ''Tweaking the noses of Muslims ... has never struck me as anything other than a vapid way to use the pen ... I affirm our right to 'take the piss' ... but we can try to think why the world is the way it is...''
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joe Sacco's reflection: good satire should probe causes, context, and power relations rather than offering empty provocation. Scoring note: greater weight to satire that informs or invites reflection versus mere insult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial decision-making about republishing controversial images
rubrics_metrics.description: Some media republished the cartoons immediately; others covered the story without showing the drawings; the BBC reviewed previous guidelines against depictions of Muhammad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical editorial criterion: weigh public interest, legal/guideline constraints, audience sensitivities, and safety when deciding whether to republish controversial depictions. Examples: Bloomberg, The Huffington Post, Gawker republished; The New York Times and others did not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider safety and likely consequences when publishing controversial material
rubrics_metrics.description: After republishing/reprinting of cartoons and as a consequence of provocative content, media outlets and individuals faced threats, firebombing, arrests and violence; some staff required police protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational guideline: assess credible threats and potential harm (to staff, distribution points, communities) when publishing; implement security measures or decline publication if risks are unmanageable. Example: P-Magazine staff in Belgium were given police protection; Hamburger Morgenpost office was fire-bombed after republication.
